level.title: Advanced SQL & Data Wrangling
level.description: Level up your SQL beyond SELECT * — master window functions, CTEs, complex joins, and the analytical queries that power real data teams.

lessons.title: Complex Joins & Subqueries
lessons.content_md:
# Complex Joins & Subqueries

Basic joins get you started. Complex joins and subqueries make you dangerous.

## Join Types Refresher

| Join | Returns |
|------|---------|
| INNER JOIN | Only matching rows from both tables |
| LEFT JOIN | All rows from left + matches from right |
| RIGHT JOIN | All rows from right + matches from left |
| FULL OUTER JOIN | All rows from both tables |
| CROSS JOIN | Every combination (cartesian product) |

## Self Joins

Join a table to itself. Common for hierarchical data:

```sql
-- Find each employee's manager name
SELECT 
    e.name AS employee,
    m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
```

## Anti Joins (Find Missing Data)

Find rows in one table that have NO match in another:

```sql
-- Customers who have never placed an order
SELECT c.name, c.email
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
```

## Correlated Subqueries

A subquery that references the outer query — executed once per outer row:

```sql
-- Employees earning more than their department average
SELECT name, salary, department_id
FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary)
    FROM employees
    WHERE department_id = e.department_id
);
```

## EXISTS vs IN

```sql
-- EXISTS: more efficient for large subquery results
SELECT name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o 
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id 
    AND o.total > 1000
);

-- IN: cleaner for small lists
SELECT name FROM employees
WHERE department_id IN (
    SELECT id FROM departments WHERE location = 'NYC'
);
```

## Multi-Table Aggregation

```sql
-- Revenue by product category with customer count
SELECT 
    cat.name AS category,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS unique_customers,
    SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue,
    ROUND(AVG(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price), 2) AS avg_order_value
FROM categories cat
JOIN products p ON cat.id = p.category_id
JOIN order_items oi ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.order_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY cat.name
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC;
```

lessons.title: Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK & LAG
lessons.content_md:
# Window Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK & LAG

Window functions perform calculations **across rows related to the current row** without collapsing the result set. They're the most powerful analytical tool in SQL.

## Syntax

```sql
function_name() OVER (
    PARTITION BY column     -- group rows
    ORDER BY column         -- sort within group
    ROWS/RANGE frame        -- optional window frame
)
```

## ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK

```sql
SELECT 
    name,
    department,
    salary,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS row_num,
    RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rank,
    DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rank
FROM employees;
```

| name | department | salary | row_num | rank | dense_rank |
|------|-----------|--------|---------|------|------------|
| Alice | Engineering | 120k | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| Bob | Engineering | 120k | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| Carol | Engineering | 110k | 3 | 3 | 2 |

**Difference:** RANK skips numbers after ties; DENSE_RANK doesn't.

## Top-N Per Group

The classic interview question — get the top 3 earners per department:

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT *,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rn
    FROM employees
)
SELECT name, department, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3;
```

## LAG & LEAD (Access Adjacent Rows)

```sql
-- Month-over-month revenue change
SELECT 
    month,
    revenue,
    LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
    revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change,
    ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) 
          / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS pct_change
FROM monthly_revenue;
```

| month | revenue | prev_month | change | pct_change |
|-------|---------|-----------|--------|------------|
| Jan | 100k | NULL | NULL | NULL |
| Feb | 120k | 100k | 20k | 20.0% |
| Mar | 108k | 120k | -12k | -10.0% |

## Running Totals & Moving Averages

```sql
SELECT 
    date,
    daily_sales,
    SUM(daily_sales) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS running_total,
    AVG(daily_sales) OVER (
        ORDER BY date 
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    ) AS moving_avg_7d
FROM sales;
```

## NTILE (Percentile Buckets)

```sql
-- Divide customers into 4 spending quartiles
SELECT 
    name,
    total_spent,
    NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total_spent DESC) AS quartile
FROM customers;
```

lessons.title: CTEs & Modular Query Design
lessons.content_md:
# CTEs & Modular Query Design

Common Table Expressions (CTEs) are temporary named result sets that make complex queries readable, maintainable, and debuggable.

## Basic CTE Syntax

```sql
WITH cte_name AS (
    SELECT ...
)
SELECT * FROM cte_name;
```

## Why CTEs Beat Subqueries

**Without CTE (nested subquery hell):**
```sql
SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT * FROM (
        SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS lifetime_value
        FROM orders
        GROUP BY customer_id
    ) sub1
    WHERE lifetime_value > 1000
) sub2
JOIN customers c ON sub2.customer_id = c.id;
```

**With CTEs (clean and readable):**
```sql
WITH customer_value AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id, 
        SUM(total) AS lifetime_value
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
high_value AS (
    SELECT * FROM customer_value
    WHERE lifetime_value > 1000
)
SELECT 
    c.name,
    c.email,
    hv.lifetime_value
FROM high_value hv
JOIN customers c ON hv.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY hv.lifetime_value DESC;
```

## Chaining Multiple CTEs

Build analysis step by step:

```sql
WITH 
-- Step 1: Daily revenue
daily_rev AS (
    SELECT 
        DATE(order_date) AS day,
        SUM(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY DATE(order_date)
),
-- Step 2: Add 7-day moving average
with_ma AS (
    SELECT 
        day,
        revenue,
        AVG(revenue) OVER (
            ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
        ) AS ma_7d
    FROM daily_rev
),
-- Step 3: Flag anomalies
anomalies AS (
    SELECT *,
        CASE WHEN revenue > ma_7d * 1.5 THEN 'SPIKE'
             WHEN revenue < ma_7d * 0.5 THEN 'DROP'
             ELSE 'NORMAL'
        END AS flag
    FROM with_ma
)
SELECT * FROM anomalies WHERE flag != 'NORMAL';
```

## Recursive CTEs

For hierarchical data like org charts or category trees:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE org_chart AS (
    -- Base case: CEO (no manager)
    SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS depth
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    
    UNION ALL
    
    -- Recursive case: find reports
    SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id, oc.depth + 1
    FROM employees e
    JOIN org_chart oc ON e.manager_id = oc.id
)
SELECT 
    REPEAT('  ', depth - 1) || name AS org_tree,
    depth
FROM org_chart
ORDER BY depth, name;
```

## CTE Best Practices

| Practice | Why |
|----------|-----|
| Name CTEs descriptively | `high_value_customers` not `cte1` |
| One logical step per CTE | Easier to debug |
| Add comments between CTEs | Document each step |
| Test CTEs individually | `SELECT * FROM cte_name LIMIT 10` |

lessons.title: Hands-On: Analytical Dashboard Query
lessons.content_md:
# Hands-On: Analytical Dashboard Query

Build a complete executive dashboard query that a BI tool would use — combining everything from this level.

## The Scenario

You work at an e-commerce company. The CEO wants a single query that shows:
- Monthly revenue with month-over-month growth
- Top 5 products per month
- Customer retention metrics

## Part 1: Monthly Revenue & Growth

```sql
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
    SELECT 
        DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
        COUNT(DISTINCT id) AS order_count,
        COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) AS unique_customers,
        SUM(total) AS revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
)
SELECT 
    month,
    revenue,
    order_count,
    unique_customers,
    LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue,
    ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)) 
          / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0), 1) AS mom_growth_pct
FROM monthly_revenue
ORDER BY month;
```

## Part 2: Top 5 Products Per Month

```sql
WITH product_monthly AS (
    SELECT 
        DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS month,
        p.name AS product,
        SUM(oi.quantity) AS units_sold,
        SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS product_revenue,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
            PARTITION BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)
            ORDER BY SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) DESC
        ) AS rank
    FROM order_items oi
    JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
    JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
    GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date), p.name
)
SELECT month, product, units_sold, product_revenue
FROM product_monthly
WHERE rank <= 5
ORDER BY month, rank;
```

## Part 3: Cohort Retention

```sql
WITH first_purchase AS (
    SELECT 
        customer_id,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_month
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY customer_id
),
cohort_activity AS (
    SELECT 
        fp.cohort_month,
        DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date) AS activity_month,
        COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS active_customers
    FROM orders o
    JOIN first_purchase fp ON o.customer_id = fp.customer_id
    GROUP BY fp.cohort_month, DATE_TRUNC('month', o.order_date)
),
cohort_size AS (
    SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS size
    FROM first_purchase
    GROUP BY cohort_month
)
SELECT 
    ca.cohort_month,
    ca.activity_month,
    cs.size AS cohort_size,
    ca.active_customers,
    ROUND(100.0 * ca.active_customers / cs.size, 1) AS retention_pct
FROM cohort_activity ca
JOIN cohort_size cs ON ca.cohort_month = cs.cohort_month
ORDER BY ca.cohort_month, ca.activity_month;
```

## What You Built

| Dashboard Section | Techniques Used |
|-------------------|----------------|
| Revenue trend | CTE, LAG, aggregation |
| Top products | Window function, ROW_NUMBER, PARTITION BY |
| Cohort retention | Multiple CTEs, self-join, percentage calculation |

This is exactly how analytics engineers at companies like Airbnb, Spotify, and Stripe structure their dashboard queries.

## Challenge

Add a fourth section: **customer lifetime value (LTV)** grouped by acquisition channel. Hint: use NTILE(4) to bucket customers into LTV quartiles.
